title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment
dek: RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
why: High information density: Diogo breaks down the trade-offs between RLHF, RLVR, and RLCD in detail, suited to anyone who needs to form a judgment on model training directions.
who: Engineers and founders focused on model training directions, RLHF/RLVR trade-offs, and the shape of AI infrastructure.
skip: After 2:18:40, the chat about European servers and hiring can be skipped.

points.h: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
points.body: Diogo argues no one pays attention to RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without errors, the model must be extremely conservative, because errors are immediately visible while subtly wrong but plausible-looking outputs are hard to spot; this calibration is "total poison" to the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart showing "LLMs necessarily fail as sequences get longer" is mathematically obvious but empirically false—when you cover the distribution you aren't over-penalized by outliers; mode drop is what loses the minority classes.

points.h: Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety issue
points.body: Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is "doing what the user wants," the former is "following someone else's instructions," like OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it is "nuts," "completely unacceptable"—if a dependency runs in the background, having software randomly crash because a user sent a weird message is insanity. He opposes adding restrictions at the technical layer, on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence further, and today's models are already fractured enough.

points.h: Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
points.body: Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had teams dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to boost scores, essentially "benchmarking with extra steps." He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but long term you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a specific workflow and evaluate it there. He also says if they wanted to make Jev dumber, they could have shipped it a year and a half ago.

points.h: RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
points.body: Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, then learning to summarize, and only later instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is "the North Star of instruction following," unrelated to the PPO algorithm—just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm yet still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

points.h: Reliability is a catchall; the North Star is robustness
points.body: Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, it ultimately comes down to some kind of reliability problem—maybe type safety, maybe determinism, maybe just the model being too jagged. He explicitly opposes treating determinism (same input, same output) as the North Star, arguing it's only slightly valuable for unit tests; what really matters is robustness—similar inputs yielding similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says when people get burned by AI decisions, that's exactly where robustness fails.

points.h: Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
points.body: Diogo thinks the industry is focusing on the wrong things: "people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability." His judgment is that reliability is what makes people delighted and what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth—he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that is the mark of an economic revolution, and what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all current models are still roughly at zero on valuable work in the world economy, maybe not even 1%.

points.h: The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
points.body: Diogo says outright that for a model shaped like TypeSafe's, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not "RLVR is useless," but that the "pacing the frontier" discussion swaps the premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model "do anything they want" mid-training—the less you restrict it, the stronger it gets outside. So the danger isn't a side effect, it's the design goal. He calls this a "disillusion of responsibility": treating "we must do more RLVR" as an axiom and then concluding "we are heading toward a dangerous world."

points.h: The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
points.body: Diogo wants to explore coding agents "free from the tyranny of the KV cache." The KV cache locks you into one model; for efficiency you must keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction, decomposition—normal software practices. He uses this to explain several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents seem not to work, why compaction is a hard problem—because passing state requires intelligence far cheaper than reading state. Directions he envisions include: explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context in a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks rather than basic-ass locks.

terms.def: A model giving up generating certain reasonable but rare outputs in the name of safety, leading to a loss of diversity.
A new direction in reinforcement learning that removes humans from the feedback loop and uses programmatic signals instead.
